qdm.candidate_root_contribution: Fore-position on an ordered axis: being, coming, or placing at the front/ahead, prior to what follows — covering spatial leading-position and temporal anteriority as one axis, systematically opposed to '-x-r (behind/later).
qdm.plain_explanation: Across all 48 occurrences the root marks "the ahead-slot." Form II qaddama (27x) = cause something to occupy the slot ahead of you: deeds sent forward to meet you at reckoning (bimA qad~amat >aydiyhim, mA qad~amat li-gad 59:18), a charity presented in advance (58:12-13), nothing put forward ahead of God and His Messenger (49:1), a warning sent ahead (50:28). Form V (48:2, 74:37) = move oneself into the ahead-slot vs. lag. Form X (10:49, 16:61, 34:30, 7:34, participle 15:24) = seek to be ahead of an appointed point vs. seek delay. Form I: Pharaoh at the front leading his people (11:98); God advancing upon their deeds (25:23). The noun qadam/aqdAm names the fore-stepping limb — one's advanced stance — hence "make firm our feet" in confrontation (2:250, 3:147, 47:7, 8:11), a foot slipping after firmness (16:94), and qadam Sidq, a footing of truth deposited ahead with their Lord (10:2). aqdamUn (26:76) = the more-prior forefathers; qadIm (12:95, 36:39, 46:11) = long-prior, standing since before.
qdm.strongest_counterexample: 41:29 ("najAalhumA taHta aqdAminA" — beneath our feet) and 55:41 (seized by forelocks and feet): here feet are mere body parts, even the lowest point, so the fore-position residue is carried only by the lexicalized noun (the forward-stepping limb) rather than demonstrated by context. Secondary strain: 25:23 "qadimnA ilA mA amilU," where Form I reads as arrival/advancing-upon; presence requires reading it as coming into the position before/at their deeds.

lineage.plain_explanation: Across all 48 occurrences the root marks "the ahead-slot." Form II qaddama (27x) = cause something to occupy the slot ahead of you: deeds sent forward to meet you at reckoning (bimA qad~amat >aydiyhim, mA qad~amat li-gad 59:18), a charity presented in advance (58:12-13), nothing put forward ahead of God and His Messenger (49:1), a warning sent ahead (50:28). Form V (48:2, 74:37) = move oneself into the ahead-slot vs. lag. Form X (10:49, 16:61, 34:30, 7:34, participle 15:24) = seek to be ahead of an appointed point vs. seek delay. x$y.candidate_root_contribution: Apprehension proportioned to the appraised weight of its object: an estimation-grounded, object-directed fear of a source or eventuality judged to have power over one's outcomes, which operates without the threat being perceptually present (بالغيب, أن-clauses about projected futures) and which regulates present conduct (withholding, yielding, compliance, preemptive action).
x$y.plain_explanation: Across all 48 occurrences, خشي is never fear of a present, perceived danger; it is always apprehension keyed to an APPRAISAL of what its object could do or bring about. Three corpus-internal signals establish this. (1) Knowledge-linkage: 35:28 makes خشية of God the mark of العلماء specifically; 79:19 sequences guidance-to-the-Lord then فتخشى; the reminder cluster (20:3, 20:44, 79:26, 87:10) treats خشية as the receptivity that a تذكرة/عبرة activates. Fear here follows from knowing/estimating the object's weight. (2) Absence-compatibility: خشية repeatedly takes unseen or future objects — the Lord بالغيب (21:49, 35:18, 36:11, 50:33, 67:12), a Day (31:33), the Hour (79:45), and projected eventualities via أن-clauses (18:80, 20:94, 5:52) or anticipated states (إملاق 17:31, الإنفاق 17:100, كساد 9:24, العنت 4:25). (3) Conduct-regulation: خشية explains withholding spending (17:100), infanticide (17:31), hypocrites' alliances (5:52), preemptive intervention (18:80), Aaron's inaction (20:94), and is what the allocation-correction imperatives redirect (فلا تخشوهم واخشون 2:150, 5:3, 5:44; الله أحق أن تخشاه 33:37, 9:13; لم يخش إلا الله 9:18; لا يخشون أحدا إلا الله 33:39). Because it is appraisal-based, it is gradable and comparable (4:77 كخشية الله أو أشد خشية) and can be misallocated — the corpus's recurrent polemic is precisely about re-ranking whose weight one apprehends. The inanimate cases (stones falling من خشية الله 2:74; the mountain crumbling 59:21) confirm the residue is response-to-appraised-overwhelming-weight rather than a merely human emotion.
x$y.strongest_counterexample: 18:80 (فخشينا أن يرهقهما طغيانا وكفرا): the speaker is the "We" of the Khidr narrative, and attributing a raw fear-emotion there strains. It is reconciled only under the appraisal-based formulation — an estimation of a weighty projected outcome motivating preemptive action — whose أن-clause construction exactly parallels the uncontroversial human cases 20:94 (خشيت أن تقول) and 5:52 (نخشى أن تصيبنا). Secondary pressure comes from 2:74 and 59:21 (stones/mountain من خشية الله), where "anticipation of future harm" strains but "yielding response to appraised overwhelming weight" holds; these two cases actively support the weight-appraisal residue over a narrow emotion reading.

Ejl.candidate_root_contribution: Forward displacement in time relative to a due term: bringing about, seeking, or embodying the arrival of something BEFORE its appointed/completed measure (the counter-pole of >jl 'appointed term' and t-A-x-r 'deferral').
Ejl.plain_explanation: Across all 47 occurrences the root marks not mere speed but prematurity — something pulled ahead of a set point of completion. Form X (19x + its verbal noun) is always "demanding God's threatened decree arrive before its term," and the verses themselves supply the term being violated (ajal musamman 29:53, ajaluhum 10:11, maw'id 18:58, qabla yawmi al-hisab 38:16, min qabli an yuqda ilayka wahyuhu 20:114). Form II is delivering a thing early (advance payment of this-life share 17:18, early portion of promised spoils 48:20). The base verb is acting ahead of a running count or an incomplete process (19:84, 20:84, 75:16). al-'ajilah is "the life that arrives first" opposed to the deferred heavy day (76:27). 'ajal (21:37) names the disposition itself, with explicit root wordplay. The calf ('ijl, 10x) reads as the pre-mature bovine, and the Quran itself welds the idol-calf to root-haste verbs: a'jalaka/'ajiltu (20:83-84) directly precede the calf of 20:88, and 7:150 indicts the calf-takers with a-'ajiltum amra rabbikum — the calf is the artifact of not waiting out the forty appointed nights (2:51).
Ejl.strongest_counterexample: 'ijl "calf" (esp. 11:69, 51:26 where it is simply food offered to guests): the lexeme could be a semantically opaque animal name (a homonym or borrowing) with no live temporal content. It is reconciled as "the not-yet-mature bovine" plus the packet-internal coupling of the calf narrative to root-haste verbs (20:83-88, 7:150, 2:51's forty nights; even 11:69 is framed by fa-ma labitha and 51:26 by faragha), but the temporal residue in the bare noun is plausible rather than independently demonstrable from verse text alone.

bdA.candidate_root_contribution: First-onset: performing the initial instance of an act or process, occupying the first position in an ordered (and typically iterable) sequence — an onset defined relative to what follows it (a next stage, a repetition, or a return).
bdA.plain_explanation: Across all 15 occurrences, b-d-ʾ marks "doing X for the first time / as the first step." Ten tokens sit in the creation formula "He begins the creation, then repeats it" (10:4, 10:34 twice, 21:104, 27:64, 29:19, 29:20, 30:11, 30:27, 32:7), where the root supplies the first pass of a process whose second pass is named by ʿ-w-d or by "the latter production" (29:20). The two human-agent uses make the ordinal sense explicit: Joseph "began with their bags BEFORE his brother's bag" (12:76) — first item in a series — and the enemies "initiated against you THE FIRST TIME" (9:13). The absolute uses (85:13 "He originates and repeats", 7:29 "as He first made you, you will return") and the negation (34:49 "falsehood neither originates nor repeats") trade on the same first-versus-again polarity. The root never describes the manner of making — only that this is the first performance.
bdA.strongest_counterexample: 12:76 (فَبَدَأَ بِأَوْعِيَتِهِمْ قَبْلَ وِعَاءِ أَخِيهِ): the only occurrence with no repetition or return anywhere in view — the search is a one-time event. It falsifies any residue phrased as "onset destined for repetition." It is reconciled only under the weaker, ordinal formulation ("first position in an ordered sequence," here marked by qabla), which is why the residue was framed that way.

byE.candidate_root_contribution: A ratified reciprocal hand-over: two parties each relinquish something of value to the other under agreed terms, sealing a binding, finalized exchange-compact (whether the counter-values are goods/price or selves-and-allegiance/reward-and-protection).
byE.plain_explanation: Across all 15 occurrences the root marks a two-sided, terms-bearing, sealed exchange. As a bare noun (bayʿ) it names the finalized exchange-event itself: the commercial transaction that ceases on the Last Day (2:254, 14:31), that is licit as against ribā (2:275 twice), that must not distract from or displace remembrance and prayer (24:37, 62:9), and — decisively for the unity claim — the exchange with God in which believers hand over selves and wealth against the Garden (9:111 bi-bayʿikum, explicitly glossed by the verse itself with ishtarā, 'purchased'). Form III (bāyaʿa, 6x: 48:10 twice, 48:18, 60:12 twice, 9:111) is the same exchange directed at a personal counterpart: the pledge scenes, where the hand-imagery is explicit ('the hand of God is above their hands', 48:10) and the terms are itemized ('pledge you ON the condition that they not associate...', 60:12) — allegiance and obedience handed over against acceptance, forgiveness, and reward. Form VI (tabāyaʿtum, 2:282) is the mutual enactment among ordinary parties, embedded in a passage about debts, terms, and witnessing — again exchange-with-ratification (witnesses seal it). The one resistant item is 22:40 (biyaʿ, plural), which denotes a class of worship-buildings; there the root contribution survives only as naming motivation: houses in which the God-ward exchange-compact (the sense fixed internally by 9:111 and 48:10) is enacted and God's name remembered — coherent, but not demonstrably a live synchronic semantics of the word.
byE.strongest_counterexample: 22:40 — biyaʿ appears in a list of demolishable buildings (ṣawāmiʿ, biyaʿ, ṣalawāt, masājid) 'in which God's name is much remembered'. The word denotes a building-type, not an exchange-event; no transaction, parties, or terms are on the surface of the verse. The reconciliation (venues of the covenant-exchange with God) is internally motivated but inferential.

kff.candidate_root_contribution: Checking at a closed boundary: an edge or surface that arrests crossing, so that what is on one side is held from passing to the other — verbally as stopping an advancing force at the line (with ʿan marking the shielded party), nominally as the palm, the body's own stopping-and-holding surface, and in kāffah as a collective whose boundary is sealed shut (no member outside it, none detaching from it).
kff.plain_explanation: The root k-f-f is about a stopping edge. Eight verbal occurrences all describe halting something at a boundary so it cannot reach the other side: God restrains people's hands from the believers (48:20, 48:24, 5:11), restrains the Children of Israel from Jesus (5:110), may restrain the might of the disbelievers (4:84); believers are told to hold back their hands (4:77), hypocrites must withhold theirs (4:91); the disbelievers will be unable to hold the Fire back from their faces (21:39). The two noun occurrences name the palm (kaffayhi, 13:14 and 18:42) — the hand's flat checking-and-holding surface — both in scenes where it fails to retain anything (water that never reaches the mouth, wealth already lost). The five kāffah occurrences (2:208, 34:28, 9:122, 9:36 twice) describe a totality as a closed enclosure: enter peace with all of yourselves inside (2:208), fight and be fought as one unbroken body (9:36), do not march out as an undivided whole (9:122, where kāffah is explicitly opposed to a detached faction), and a mission whose reach closes around all people (34:28). One idea — a boundary that lets nothing cross — runs through restraining, the palm, and totality.
kff.strongest_counterexample: The kāffah cluster, sharpest at 2:208 'udkhulū fī s-silmi kāffatan' — 'enter into peace kāffah' reads on the surface as plain 'entirely/all together,' with no visible act of restraint, and could be claimed as a lexicalized adverb detached from the root. Resolution from inside the corpus: 9:122 opposes kāffah to a firqah/ṭāʾifah that separates out, and 2:208 immediately opposes it to following Satan's khuṭuwāt (step-by-step leakage out of the whole) — kāffah is totality construed as a sealed boundary, every member held within, which is the same checking-edge residue. The reconciliation works but requires this construal step, which is what caps the result at MODERATE.

mTr.candidate_root_contribution: A shower-descent from the sky onto a target below: a quantity of discrete matter (prototypically water, but substance-unspecified) falling from above in pelting, distributed fashion upon a location or people. The root encodes the manner and directionality of arrival (sky-to-ground, onto), not the substance and not any good/bad valence.
mTr.plain_explanation: In every Quranic occurrence, m-T-r is about something coming down out of the sky onto someone or something beneath it. As a plain noun it names the shower itself — ordinary rain that soldiers may shelter from (4:102), the rain a cloud is hoped to bring (46:24), or the terrible 'rain' that fell on Lot's people (25:40, 26:173, 27:58, 7:84). As a Form IV verb it means causing that shower to fall on a target, always with 'upon' (ʿalā): God rains stones on the condemned towns (11:82, 15:74), or mockers dare God to rain stones on them (8:32). That stones — not water — can be what is 'rained' proves the root is about the mode of falling from the sky onto a target, not about water itself; and the hopeful use in 46:24 and the neutral use in 4:102 prove the root is not inherently about punishment.
mTr.strongest_counterexample: The stone-object uses (11:82:7:2, 15:74:4:2, 8:32:11:2 — amṭarnā/fa-amṭir ʿalayhā/ʿalaynā ḥijāratan) are the hardest for any 'rain = water from the sky' reading, since what falls is stones. They are resolved, not forced: the substance is expressed in a separate object slot, so the root's own contribution must be the shower-manner of sky-to-target descent, which is demonstrably present (stones arrive exactly as a rain does — from above, in quantity, onto a target). No occurrence resists the substance-neutral shower-descent residue.

rkb.candidate_root_contribution: Superposition onto a bearer: one entity comes to be positioned on top of (or fitted onto) a distinct supporting entity that then bears/carries it. Riding is the prototypical case (rider upon animal/ship), but the residue is the mounted-upon-a-support relation itself, not motion or travel.
rkb.plain_explanation: Everywhere rkb appears, something is set upon something else that holds it up: people upon ships (11:41, 11:42, 18:71, 29:65), people upon animals (16:8, 40:79, 36:42, 43:12 — which pairs ships and cattle under one verb, showing the Quran itself treats them as one act), the nominals for mounted people and mounts (2:239 rukbaan vs. rijaal on foot, 36:72 rakuub, 59:6 rikaab, 8:42 al-rakb). The three non-riding cases carry the same relation without travel: grain mutarakib (6:99) is grains stacked one upon another; rakkabaka (82:8) is God fitting/mounting your parts together into a form; 84:19 la-tarkabunna tabaqan 'an tabaq is mounting stage upon stage, where the object tabaq (layer) itself encodes superposition. Subtract the vehicle, the journey, and the grammatical form, and the same residue remains in all fifteen.

swm.candidate_root_contribution: Setting forth into the open so as to be visibly borne: an entity is turned out into an exposed domain, or made to carry an openly displayed condition/sign that stays attached to it. The nominal siymaA is the openly borne identifying display; Form II participles denote being endowed with such a display; the Form I verb (double accusative) denotes keeping someone turned out under an imposed condition as their standing lot; Form IV denotes turning animals out into open range.
swm.plain_explanation: Across all 15 occurrences, s-w-m contributes the idea of something being put out in the open and borne there. (a) In all six siymaA tokens (2:273, 7:46, 7:48, 47:30, 48:29, 55:41) it is a visible display carried on a person by which they are recognized — five of the six collocate with the verb '-r-f "recognize" (2:273 taErifuhum bisiymaAhum; 7:46 yaErifuwna kullaan bisiymaAhum; 7:48 yaErifuwnahum bisiymaAhum; 47:30 falaEaraftahum bisiymaAhum; 55:41 yuErafu Almujrimuwna bisiymaAhum), and 48:29 locates it explicitly on the exposed surface, "siymaAhum fiy wujuwhihim min 'avari Alssujuwdi", after taraAhum "you see them". (b) The four Form II derivatives (11:83, 51:34 stones musaw~amap Einda rab~ika; 3:125 angels musaw~imiyna; 3:14 horses Almusaw~amap) denote entities made to bear such a display — the stones' marking designates them for their targets (lilmusrifiyna, 51:34). (c) The four Form I verbs (2:49, 7:141, 14:6, 7:167) all use the identical double-accusative frame yasuwmuwna-hum/yasuwmu-hum suw'a AlEa*aAbi: the victims are held turned-out under evil punishment as their imposed, continuing condition (imperfect aspect throughout; 7:167 extends it 'ilaY yawmi AlqiyaAmap). (d) The single Form IV (16:10 fiyhi tusiymuwna) is the causative of the same setting-forth: you turn livestock out into the open growth. The root residue is thus not "punish", "graze", or "sign" as such, but the open setting-forth/borne-exposure that each of those readings instantiates.
swm.strongest_counterexample: 16:10 (tusiymuwna): the pastoral token has no in-text marking or recognition dimension at all; it only fits if the residue is pitched at "turning out into the open" rather than "identifying mark". It is the occurrence that forces the abstraction level up and is therefore the best lever for falsifying the unified residue.

$yb.candidate_root_contribution: Whitening/greying of the head's hair as the visible bodily marker of depleted vitality — the chromatic sign of the late, post-strength stage of life (not old age itself, but its appearance on the head).
$yb.plain_explanation: Across all three occurrences the root supplies one thing: white/grey head-hair as the outward sign that vital strength has passed. In 19:4 Zakariyya's head has "ignited" with it alongside weakened bones; in 30:54 it names the stage after strength, conjoined with weakness; in 73:17 the terror of the Day imposes this very sign on children — they are made white-haired, not made old, which proves the root contributes the visible marker rather than chronological age.
$yb.strongest_counterexample: 73:17 is the only candidate stressor: one could claim shīb there means merely "aged ones," making the root "old age" rather than "white hair." But the verse's force is precisely the visual inversion — children bearing the white-hair sign without lived age — so the occurrence resists the "old age" reading and instead confirms the chromatic-marker residue. No occurrence is inconsistent with the proposed contribution.

*Ab.candidate_root_contribution: The wild predatory canid — the wolf as a concrete entity; in its Quranic deployment, the solitary predator whose threat attaches specifically to a human charge left without guard.
*Ab.plain_explanation: All three occurrences are the single definite noun al-dhi'b ("the wolf") inside the Yusuf narrative (12:13, 12:14, 12:17). In every occurrence the wolf is the subject of "devour" (akala) with Yusuf as object, and in every occurrence the devouring is non-actual: feared by Yaqub (12:13), hypothesized by the brothers (12:14), and falsely alleged by them (12:17). The wolf never appears on-scene; it exists only within speech about an unwitnessed event. The stable root contribution across all three is the concrete wolf-entity as the paradigmatic danger to the unguarded.
*Ab.strongest_counterexample: None exists in the confirmed set. The nearest candidate for tension is 12:17, where the wolf's act is a fabrication — but the fabricated status belongs to the speech-act context, not the root: the lie only works because the wolf-entity is a plausible devourer, which presupposes rather than contradicts the proposed contribution.

*qn.candidate_root_contribution: The chin: the frontal underside terminus of the face at its junction with the neck — the body's pivot-point that marks the extreme limit of head inclination, downward (face driven fully to the ground) or upward (head forced back so it cannot bow).
*qn.plain_explanation: All three occurrences are the same plural noun al-adhqan in a prepositional frame, and in each the chins function as a limit-line of head posture. In 17:107 and 17:109 those given knowledge "fall to the chins" (yakhirruna li-l-adhqan) — prostration pressed past the forehead to the lowest frontal point of the face, intensified by sujjadan/yabkuna/khushu'an. In 36:8 iron collars on the necks reach "up to the chins" (ila l-adhqan), so the wearers are muqmahun — heads forced up, unable to lower the face. The same referent thus anchors both extremes: chins to the ground in voluntary humility, chins propped up in enforced inability to humble. The root's contribution (the chin as the terminal frontal point of the face/head) is present and doing work in every occurrence; the polarity (down vs. up) comes from construction (li- of falling vs. ila of upper bound) and context, not from the root.
*qn.strongest_counterexample: 36:8 is the only candidate for resistance: chins there are pushed UP, the apparent opposite of the falling-down usage in 17:107/109. But the root supplies the same referent in both; the opposed directions come from ila (collar's upper limit) vs. kharra li- (collapse onto), so 36:8 confirms rather than breaks the residue — the chin is precisely the line the collar must reach to prevent the bowing that 17:107/109 describe. No occurrence resists the proposed contribution.

*rw.candidate_root_contribution: A sweeping, wind-like agency that lifts light or loose matter and carries it away into scattered, irrecoverable dispersion (winnowing-away): the event necessarily involves (a) a moving carrier-agent, (b) a light/particulate patient, and (c) an endpoint of dissipation rather than placement.
*rw.plain_explanation: All three occurrences describe the same event seen through different grammatical lenses. In 18:45 the winds (explicit agent الرياح) sweep away dried plant debris (هشيم) — the verb تذروه with its object suffix shows a transitive act of carrying-off-into-dispersion, sealing the parable of worldly life ending in dissipation. In 51:1 the same event is packaged twice: الذاريات is the agent-participle ('the ones who scatter-carry', internally identifiable as winds via the 18:45 parallel, the only other root occurrence), and ذروا is the cognate masdar intensifying that very event. Subtract the oath construction and the parable context and the identical residue remains in every token.
*rw.strongest_counterexample: None found in the full set. The nearest candidate for resistance is 51:1 الذاريات, whose referent is not named in the verse; but the root contribution itself is secured internally by the exact agent-verb parallel in 18:45 (الرياح ... تذروه), and the cognate accusative ذروا confirms the event-type independent of referent identification. It does not break universal presence.

ASr.candidate_root_contribution: A binding constraint imposed on a bearer from outside: an obligation experienced as a tying load that rests upon the one bound, laid on, contracted, or lifted off by another party.
ASr.plain_explanation: In all three Quranic occurrences, iṣr names something that sits *upon* a party and both weighs on them and binds them. In 2:286 it is a load a Lord may lay upon a community (ḥamala ʿalā), as on earlier communities; in 3:81 it is the binding grip of God's covenant that the prophets take upon themselves by affirming; in 7:157 it is what the Messenger lifts off his followers, paired with shackles (aghlāl). The root's contribution is the fusion of burden and bond: an imposed obligation felt as a constraining weight — never a self-acquired load (that is wizr) and never the pact-event itself (that is mīthāq).
ASr.strongest_counterexample: 3:81 (word_ref 3:81:25:1) is the most resistant: a plain 'heavy burden' reading is strained there, since iṣrī denotes the covenant commitment the prophets affirm. It is reconciled without forcing because the covenant is explicitly taken ʿalā ('upon') them — the residue 'imposed binding constraint resting on a bearer' is demonstrably present; only the pure-weight competitor fails, not the proposed residue.

Abl.candidate_root_contribution: Massed aggregation: a plurality of living units apprehended and handled as one collective body (herd/swarm/wave-mass), such that the many are construed grammatically and referentially as a single unit.
Abl.plain_explanation: The root surfaces in two lexemes: al-'ibil "the camel-kind" (6:144, 88:17) and abaabiil "in massed groups" (105:3). What survives subtraction of form and context in all three is not "camel" (birds in 105:3 refute that) but aggregation-as-unity. In 105:3 birds are sent as massed groups acting en bloc; in 88:17 the plural referent takes a feminine SINGULAR verb (khuliqat — "how IT was created"), showing the multitude construed as one body; in 6:144 the collective class is treated as a single countable kind ("of the 'ibil, two") in parallel with other livestock classes. Every occurrence presents many members packaged as one collective.
Abl.strongest_counterexample: 6:144 is the weakest link for the aggregation hypothesis: the verse itself foregrounds the camel-kind only as a legal category alongside al-baqar, and the aggregation feature is present only via the collective-noun grammar, with no contextual foregrounding of herd-ness. Against the rival "camel-kind" hypothesis, 105:3 (tayran abaabiil — birds, not camels) is a decisive counterexample.

Aff.candidate_root_contribution: A vocalized burst of aversion/displeasure — the minimal audible ejaculation by which a speaker vents exasperation, irritation, or repugnance toward the person or thing it is aimed at.
Aff.plain_explanation: The root surfaces in all three occurrences as one and the same lexical interjection, أُفٍّ ("uff"), an exclamatory noise of displeasure. In 17:23 the son is forbidden to so much as say أُفٍّ to aged parents ("فَلَا تَقُل لَّهُمَآ أُفٍّ") — here the utterance is the smallest conceivable audible sign of impatience/annoyance, set in a chain with تَنْهَرْهُمَا (rebuking) as an escalation of the same aversion. In 21:67 Abraham hurls "أُفٍّ لَّكُمْ وَلِمَا تَعْبُدُونَ مِن دُونِ ٱللَّهِ" at his people and their idols — the same interjection venting disgust/repudiation. In 46:17 the impious son answers his parents "أُفٍّ لَّكُمَآ أَتَعِدَانِنِىٓ..." — venting exasperated rejection at their warning of resurrection. Across mild filial impatience (17:23), prophetic contempt (21:67), and rebellious exasperation (46:17), the invariant the root itself supplies is the spontaneous expulsion of displeasure as a cry — not a proposition, not a verb of action, but an affect-laden exclamation of aversion.
Aff.strongest_counterexample: 17:23 is the hardest case because the displeasure there is minimal and directed at beloved, honored parents — closer to weary impatience than to the contempt seen in 21:67/46:17. It reconciles cleanly: the verse works precisely by treating أُفٍّ as the smallest possible audible expression of displeasure (its prohibition is a fortiori — if even that tiny vent is barred, harsher speech certainly is). Far from breaking the core, it fixes the lower bound of the same aversion-venting residue.

Afq.candidate_root_contribution: The outer bounding rim/verge of the visible spatial expanse — the far encompassing edge where the seen field terminates (the "horizon"), conceived as the outermost perimeter of the observable world.
Afq.plain_explanation: All three occurrences are the same noun (QAC tag N), the horizon-word, in two morphological shapes: the plural ٱلْـَٔافَاق (41:53) and the singular ٱلْأُفُق (53:7; 81:23). In 41:53, "We will show them Our signs فِى ٱلْـَٔافَاق (in the horizons/outer regions) وَفِىٓ أَنفُسِهِمْ (and in themselves)" — the āfāq are explicitly set OPPOSITE the inner self (anfus), so the root here contributes the OUTER encompassing expanse/verge of the world, the far bounding regions, as against the interior. In 53:7 "وَهُوَ بِٱلْأُفُقِ ٱلْأَعْلَىٰ (and he was at the highest ufuq/horizon)" and 81:23 "وَلَقَدْ رَءَاهُ بِٱلْأُفُقِ ٱلْمُبِينِ (he saw him at the clear ufuq/horizon)", the singular ufuq is the horizon-edge on which a figure appears/is seen — the outer rim of the visual field where sky meets the limit of sight. Across the plural "outer regions/horizons" and the singular "horizon-rim where a figure is beheld," the invariant is the same: the outermost bounding verge of the visible expanse. Subtracting the qualifiers (ٱلْأَعْلَىٰ "highest", ٱلْمُبِين "clear/manifest") and the pluralization leaves exactly this bounding-outer-edge notion.
Afq.strongest_counterexample: 41:53 (word_ref 41:53:4:2), the plural ٱلْـَٔافَاق. It is the hardest case because, contrasted with أَنفُسِهِمْ ("their selves"), it can read as "the whole outer world/cosmos" broadly rather than narrowly "the horizon-rim," tempting a wider "external world" gloss. It reconciles cleanly: the plural of ufuq is precisely the far outer horizons/regions that bound and encompass the world; the outer-vs-inner contrast (āfāq vs anfus) actually confirms the root's "outer encompassing verge" contribution rather than defeating it. The extension from "edge" to "outer regions" is the ordinary semantic effect of pluralizing a boundary-rim noun, not a different root sense.

Ajj.candidate_root_contribution: The root marks water (a potable-substance) as carrying an intense, biting bitter-salt harshness — the quality of being so pungently briny that it repels consumption. It is the negative sensory pole of drinkable water: the property of being harsh/undrinkable rather than merely "salt as a substance."
Ajj.plain_explanation: Every one of the three occurrences is the same lexeme أُجَاج (ujāj), all tagged form N, and all predicated of water. In 25:53:10:1 and 35:12:11:1 the word stands in an explicit antithetical pair: one sea is عَذْبٌ فُرَاتٌ (sweet, fresh) — in 35:12 further glossed سَآئِغٌ شَرَابُهُ (its drink slips down pleasantly) — and the other is مِلْحٌ أُجَاجٌ. Crucially أُجَاج is appended AFTER مِلْح (salt): the substance-word "salt" is already present, so أُجَاج is not supplying the bare fact of salt but intensifying/qualifying it as bitingly briny and undrinkable. In 56:70:4:1 the word appears alone, without مِلْح: "if We willed We could have made it (the water they drink, from the preceding verse) أُجَاجًا, so why are you not grateful?" Here أُجَاج by itself carries the whole load — spoiled, undrinkable brine set against the freshwater they actually receive. Across all three, subtracting the drinkable/fresh counterpart leaves one invariant: the root contributes the harsh bitter-salt quality that makes water unfit to drink.
Ajj.strongest_counterexample: 56:70:4:1 (جَعَلْنَٰهُ أُجَاجًا) is the hardest because it lacks the مِلْح ("salt") that anchors the sense in the other two, and because it is a predicate of جَعَلَ rather than an attribute — one could worry the meaning is being imported from the sister verses. It reconciles cleanly: the immediately preceding verses (56:68-69) speak of the fresh water they drink and its heaven-sent source, so أُجَاج stands as the antithetical spoiled/undrinkable outcome. That the word alone, without مِلْح, still denotes undrinkable brine actually strengthens the residue — it shows the harsh-briny-unfitness is carried by the root itself and not borrowed from the noun "salt."

Anf.candidate_root_contribution: The foremost / leading front-extremity of an entity — its protruding front-point taken as the salient forward edge (spatially: the projecting front of the face = the nose; extended temporally: the leading, immediately-adjacent edge of just-elapsed time = "just now").
Anf.plain_explanation: Only two surface senses appear across the three occurrences. (A) In 5:45 (words 9:3 وَٱلْأَنفَ and 10:3 بِٱلْأَنفِ) the form is the concrete noun ٱلْأَنف "the nose," embedded in the lex-talionis catalogue النفس بالنفس ... والأنف بالأنف "the nose for the nose." The referent is the anatomical organ that is, physically, the frontmost projecting feature of the face. (B) In 47:16 (word 16:1) the form is the active-participle-adverbial ءَانِفًا in مَاذَا قَالَ ءَانِفًا "what did he say just now / a moment ago" — a temporal adverb pointing to the immediately preceding instant. The only abstraction that could unify both is a domain-neutral notion of "foremost/leading front-point": the nose as the forward projection of the face, and "just now" as the leading/nearest front-edge of elapsed time. But note that in NEITHER occurrence is this abstract "front-point" residue surface-present: in (A) the surface value is simply "nose," and in (B) it is simply "recently." The connecting schema must be supplied by inference, not read off the text.
Anf.strongest_counterexample: 47:16:16:1 (ءَانِفًا). The two 5:45 tokens are mutually consistent (both = "nose," the front-projecting facial organ) and can each carry a "foremost front-point" reading with only mild inference. ءَانِفًا cannot: its determinate surface value is purely temporal ("just now / a moment ago"), and recovering the "foremost/front" residue from it requires a spatial→temporal metaphor (front-in-space → nearest-in-past-time). No occurrence in the packet displays that spatial-to-temporal bridge, so the metaphor is externally/etymologically motivated, not internally attested. It therefore stays unreconciled by pure layer-subtraction.

Ass.candidate_root_contribution: The load-bearing GROUNDING BASE — the invariant is the notion of a supporting foundation/bottom-set upon which a raised structure is grounded and from which it takes its stability. The root supplies specifically the base-that-underlies-and-supports, not the edifice itself and not the mere act of building.
Ass.plain_explanation: The root occurs only in one form-family here: the Form II verb أسّس ("to found / lay the base of"), 3 times, all in Surah 9:108–109. In 9:109 the same verb is repeated in explicit antithesis: أفمن أسّس بُنيانه على تقوى ... أم من أسّس بُنيانه على شفا جُرُف هار — "is he who FOUNDED his building upon God-consciousness ... or he who FOUNDED his building upon the brink of a crumbling cliff?" Here the root's contribution is isolated with unusual clarity because the OBJECT of the verb is بُنيان (the built structure, root b-n-y) and the verb أسّس names the distinct act of setting that structure's supporting BASE. The عَلَى-phrase names WHAT the base rests on (firm taqwā vs. an undercut cliff-edge that then collapses, فانهار به), and the whole point of the contrast is the quality of the grounding-base: a sound base holds, an unsound base gives way. The passive at 9:108, لمسجدٌ أُسِّسَ على التقوى من أول يوم ("a mosque whose base was laid upon God-consciousness from the very first day"), shows the same residue under voice-change: a structure is grounded upon a supporting base from its origin. Across all three, subtract morphology and only the grounding-base concept remains constant.
Ass.strongest_counterexample: The passive 9:108:6:1 (أُسِّسَ على التقوى من أول يوم) is the hardest, because the added phrase مِن أول يوم ("from the first day") could tempt a reading of the root as "to begin/originate." But it reconciles cleanly: the root still denotes the base-laying event; "from the first day" is a temporal adjunct locating WHEN the base was laid, and the structure named (مسجد) still stands ON that base (على التقوى). The originative flavor is contributed by the temporal phrase plus the intrinsic once-for-all nature of foundation-laying, not by the root, which retains its grounding-base sense identically to the active pair in 9:109.

Aty.candidate_root_contribution: Directed, completive ARRIVAL AT A DESIGNATED TERMINUS: some entity — a person, event, message, thing, or conferred good — comes-to and REACHES a goal-point (a person, place, time, act, or state). Form I predicates the entity's own arrival at the goal; Form I + bi- and the causative Form IV (آتى / يؤتي) add an agent who makes an object arrive at a recipient, i.e. "bring / produce / hand-over / bestow / render-a-due." The invariant left in every token is the reaching-of-a-terminus (causatively: the making-reach).
Aty.plain_explanation: The 549 tokens split by morphology into two branches that share one core. FORM I = intransitive arrival: "أَتَىٰ أَمْرُ ٱللَّهِ" the command of God has come (16:1); "أَتَىٰهَآ أَمْرُنَا" Our decree came to it (10:24); "فَلَمَّآ أَتَىٰهَا" when Moses came to the fire (20:11); "يَوْمَ يَأْتِيهِمُ ٱلْعَذَابُ" the day the punishment comes to them (14:44); "مَن يَأْتِ رَبَّهُۥ مُجْرِمًا" whoever comes to his Lord as a sinner (20:74); "هَلْ أَتَىٰكَ حَدِيثُ مُوسَىٰ" has the account of Moses come to you (79:15); "أَتَتْ عَلَيْهِ" the wind comes upon it (51:42); "هَلْ أَتَىٰ عَلَى ٱلْإِنسَٰنِ حِينٌ" has a span of time come upon man (76:1). FORM I + bi- = bring/produce (cause-to-come-along): "فَأْتُوا۟ بِسُورَةٍ" bring a sura (10:38, 2:23); "ٱئْتُونِى بِهِۦ" bring him to me (12:50); "يَأْتِيكُم بِضِيَآءٍ" brings you light (28:71). FORM IV causative = give/bestow (make-arrive-at-recipient): "ءَاتَيْنَا مُوسَى ٱلْكِتَٰبَ" We gave Moses the Book (2:53); "تُؤْتِى ٱلْمُلْكَ مَن تَشَآءُ" You give kingship to whom You will (3:26); "ءَاتُوا۟ ٱلزَّكَوٰةَ" give the zakat (2:43); "ءَاتُوا۟ ٱلنِّسَآءَ صَدُقَٰتِهِنَّ" give the women their dowries (4:4). The two branches are proven identical by the corpus itself: 2:258 uses Form I + bi for "God brings (يَأْتِى بِـ) the sun from the east; [you] bring (فَأْتِ بِـ) it from the west," and Form IV for "give"; 24:33 "وَءَاتُوهُم مِّن مَّالِ ٱللَّهِ ٱلَّذِىٓ ءَاتَىٰكُمْ" give them of God's wealth which He gave you; 59:7 "وَمَآ ءَاتَىٰكُمُ ٱلرَّسُولُ فَخُذُوهُ" whatever the Messenger brings/gives you, take it. Passive Form IV أُوتُوا = "made to have X come to them": "ٱلَّذِينَ أُوتُوا۟ ٱلْكِتَٰبَ" those given the Book (3:19); "مَنْ أُوتِىَ كِتَٰبَهُۥ بِيَمِينِهِۦ" whoever is given his record in his right hand (69:19). Participle/verbal-noun N: "ٱلسَّاعَةَ لَـَٔاتِيَةٌ" the Hour is surely coming (15:85, 20:15, 22:7); "كُلُّهُمْ ءَاتِيهِ يَوْمَ ٱلْقِيَٰمَةِ فَرْدًا" each will come to Him alone (19:95); "كَانَ وَعْدُهُۥ مَأْتِيًّا" His promise is one that will be arrived-at/fulfilled (19:61). N(IV) verbal noun: "إِيتَآءِ ٱلزَّكَوٰةِ" the giving of zakat (16:90, 21:73, 24:37). Idiomatic "come-unto/commit": "أَتَأْتُونَ ٱلْفَٰحِشَةَ" do you come-unto the abomination (7:80, 27:54); "يَأْتِينَ بِفَٰحِشَةٍ" commit immorality (4:19); "لَا يَأْتُونَ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ إِلَّا وَهُمْ كُسَالَىٰ" they do not come to prayer except lazily (9:54). Cosmic: "ٱئْتِيَا طَوْعًا أَوْ كَرْهًا قَالَتَآ أَتَيْنَا طَآئِعِينَ" [heaven & earth] come willingly or unwillingly — they said, we come willingly (41:11). Every family reduces to arrival-at, or made-to-arrive-at, a terminus.
Aty.strongest_counterexample: The hardest tokens are Form IV bestowals of an inalienable, internal disposition, where any literal "coming/motion" is maximally bleached: 47:17:5 "وَءَاتَىٰهُمْ تَقْوَىٰهُمْ" (He gave them their piety) and 32:13:3 "لَـَٔاتَيْنَا كُلَّ نَفْسٍ هُدَىٰهَا" (We would have given every soul its guidance). Reconciliation: these are the identical double-object causative as "gave him the Book" (2:53) — the quality is made to accrue to / reach the recipient, who remains the terminus; the arrival residue here is grammatical (IV = transparent causative of أتى) rather than a felt physical motion, but it is directly corroborated by the corpus pairing Form I + bi "bring" with Form IV "give" for the very same referents (2:258 bring/give the sun; 24:33 "give of the wealth He gave you"; 59:7 "what the Messenger brings/gives you"). It reconciles without forcing. (A near-rival for the Form-I side, "بِمَآ أَتَوا۟" = what they have done/brought-about, 3:188, and "لَـَٔاتَوْهَا" = they would have committed it, 33:14, likewise reconcile as arrival-at/engagement-with an act.)

Awl.candidate_root_contribution: The root marks a PRIMARY ANCHORING TERMINUS / HEAD-POLE of a relation: the reference-point to which other elements are traced, referred, or attached. Depending only on the construction that frames it, this head-pole surfaces as (a) the origin/first term of an ordered series (أوّل / الأولى / الأوّلون), (b) the ground or resolution a sign 'reverts to' (تأويل), (c) the progenitor/head a household reverts to (آل), and (d) the bearer/holder an attribute is anchored to (أولو / أولات). The constant residue is 'the defining primary pole that a thing goes back / belongs / is referred to' — never a mid-series, dependent, or non-anchoring member.
Awl.plain_explanation: Across every form-family the root contributes 'the head-anchor of a relation,' with the construction supplying which relation. (1) ORDINAL/ORIGIN pole — أوّل مرة 'the originating instance' (17:51 فطركم أوّل مرّة; 36:79; 6:94; 41:21), أوّل بيت 'the first/founding House' (3:96), أوّل يوم (9:108), أوّل المسلمين/المؤمنين/العابدين/الكافر 'the foremost/lead one' (39:12; 7:143; 43:81; 2:41), and the divine الأوّل paired with الآخر (57:3) — the origin-pole of all being. The feminine الأولى names the primary/prior member of a two-term set: المَوتة/النَّشأة/الخَلق الأولى vs الآخرة (37:59; 56:62; 50:15), الأولى والآخرة 'the first (life) and the last' (53:25; 28:70; 93:4). الأوّلون/الأوّلين = the anchor-generations of human time, 'the ancients' one traces back to (أساطير الأوّلين 8:31; سنّة الأوّلين 35:43; آباؤنا الأوّلون 37:17). (2) REVERSION-TO-GROUND pole — تأويل is the terminus a sign is referred to: of a dream/saying, its true referent/realization (تأويل الأحاديث/الأحلام 12:6, 12:21, 12:44; تأويل رؤياي 12:100), of an act, its underlying reason (18:82 ذلك تأويل ما لم تسطع), of a warning, its eschatological fulfilment (7:53 هل ينظرون إلا تأويله يوم يأتي تأويله; 10:39), of an ambiguous verse, its ground of meaning (3:7), and أحسن تأويلا 'best in final outcome' (17:35; 4:59). Note the pole here sits at the END/ground rather than the beginning — the same 'terminus one reverts to,' the classical آل يؤول. (3) PROGENITOR-HEAD pole — آل X = the folk defined by anchoring to a named head: آل فرعون (2:49; 7:130; 40:46), آل لوط (15:59), آل يعقوب/إبراهيم/عمران (19:6; 4:54; 3:33), آل داود (34:13). (4) BEARER pole — أولو/أولي/أولوا/أولات X = 'the ones to whom X is attributed/belongs': أولو الألباب 'possessors of understanding' (2:269; 3:190; 39:9 and ~16×), أولو القوة/بأس (28:76; 27:33; 48:16), أولو الأرحام/القربى (33:6; 4:8), أولو الأمر (4:59; 4:83), أولو الأبصار/العلم/النهى (59:2; 3:18; 20:128), أولات الأحمال/حمل (65:4; 65:6). Finally the comparative أولى بـ 'nearer / having prior claim' (33:6 النبيّ أولى بالمؤمنين; 8:75 أولى ببعض) is precedence = proximity to the head-position. In every case the root names a primary anchoring pole; the frame decides whether that pole is temporal-origin, meaning-ground, progenitor, or bearer.
Awl.strongest_counterexample: The أولو/أولات 'possessors-of' family (e.g. 2:269 أولوا الألباب; 65:4 أولات الأحمال; 4:59 أولي الأمر) is the hardest, because 'possessor of X' shows no temporal firstness and looks like a bare grammatical suppletive for ذو with no distinctive root content. Reconciliation: the root still fixes the entity as the ANCHORING HEAD to which the attribute (understanding, command, wombs, a carried child) is referred/attributed — the same head-pole residue, with the genitive-attribute construction (not the root) supplying the possessive rather than the temporal reading. This is genuine but the most inferential link, which is why the disposition is MODERATE, not STRONG. A secondary hard case, تأويل as eschatological outcome (7:53 يوم يأتي تأويله), puts the pole at the END rather than the beginning; but this is reconciled by design, since the invariant is 'terminus one reverts to,' which the data itself lets sit at either the origin (أوّل) or the resolution (تأويل).

Azf.candidate_root_contribution: The root contributes the notion of IMMINENT TEMPORAL DRAWING-NEAR: an appointed event pressing close / becoming at-hand in time. The invariant is not mere spatial or generic nearness but the impending, urgent approach of a fixed moment that is on the verge of arriving.
Azf.plain_explanation: Only two verses carry the root, and one of them holds two of the three occurrences, which lets internal evidence arbitrate cleanly. In 53:57 the finite verb and the participle stand side by side: أَزِفَتِ ٱلْـَٔازِفَةُ — "the Āzifah has drawn near." The verb أَزِفَتْ (form I perfect) supplies the surface-explicit predicate "has drawn near / become imminent," and its subject ٱلْآزِفَةُ is the active participle from the same root used substantively as an epithet ("the Approaching / Impending one"). The fact that the root is predicated of its own participle — "the Approaching has approached" — shows the live charge is the ACT of temporal approach, not an emptied label. In 40:18, يَوْمَ ٱلْآزِفَةِ ("the Day of the Āzifah") uses the same participle as a name for the Day of Judgment; the continuation إِذِ ٱلْقُلُوبُ لَدَى ٱلْحَنَاجِرِ (hearts reaching the throats) frames it as an impending, pressing crisis. Across all three, subtracting the eschatological referent (the Hour/Day) leaves the same residue: something is on the point of arriving, temporally at hand.
Azf.strongest_counterexample: The hardest case is 40:18:3:2, يَوْمَ ٱلْآزِفَةِ, where ٱلْآزِفَة functions as a fixed proper-name epithet for the Day of Judgment. One could argue the root here has bleached into a mere label ("the Hour"), losing the "approaching" content. It reconciles decisively via internal evidence: 53:57 predicates the verb أَزِفَتْ ("has drawn near") OF this very same participle ٱلْآزِفَةُ. That predication would be tautological/vacuous if the participle meant only "the Hour"; it is coherent only if the participle still carries "the Approaching one." So the naming use in 40:18 is a transparent derivation from the live sense of temporal approach, not a break from it.

Dgv.candidate_root_contribution: A handful-sized clump of multiple heterogeneous strands grasped/gathered together into one bound bundle; hence, by extension, a tangle of disparate elements jumbled into a single unsorted mass.
Dgv.plain_explanation: Only 3 occurrences, all nominal (form N), and they split into two sense-families that both resolve to one image. (1) 38:44 gives the concrete, surface sense: "وَخُذْ بِيَدِكَ ضِغْثًا فَٱضْرِب بِّهِ" — Job is told to take in his hand a ḍighth and strike with it. A ḍighth is precisely a handful/bunch — a bundle of stalks or twigs gathered together into one graspable clump. The word denotes the bound, hand-sized aggregate of several strands, not a single item. (2) 12:44 and 21:5 give the plural أَضْغَاث in the fixed phrase "أَضْغَٰثُ أَحْلَٰمٍ" — the king's dream (12:44) and the Prophet's revelation (21:5) are dismissed as "aḍghāth of dreams," i.e. a tangled bundle of mixed dream-fragments, incoherent precisely because it is a heap of disparate strands with no single sortable thread. The invariant across all three is the "bound clump of many mixed strands": literally a fistful of stalks (38:44), metaphorically a fistful of jumbled dream-material (12:44, 21:5). The "confusedness" foregrounded in the dream verses is not an extra root meaning but the natural effect of the root's own image — heterogeneous strands packed into one handful cannot be told apart.
Dgv.strongest_counterexample: 38:44 (ضِغْثًا, the handful of stalks) is the hardest because it carries none of the "confusion/incoherence" that dominates the dream verses — it is a tidy, purposeful bundle used to strike. This threatens any hypothesis that the root core is "confusedness." It reconciles cleanly, however, under the bundle reading: the root supplies "handful of gathered mixed strands," and 38:44 is exactly that at the literal level; the confusion in 12:44/21:5 is the same image applied to mental content, where a bundle of heterogeneous strands reads as an incoherent jumble. The concrete occurrence thus anchors the core and the abstract ones extend from it — no contradiction, only a determinate concrete→metaphorical direction.

DjE.candidate_root_contribution: The settling of a body — specifically its side/trunk — down into a recumbent, lying-flat position against a supporting surface. The root supplies "lying-down / reclining-of-the-body," and every attested form is the noun of place (maḍjaʿ), i.e. the locus at/on which that recumbency occurs.
DjE.plain_explanation: All 3 occurrences are morphologically identical: the maf'al noun-of-place from ض ج ع (singular maḍjaʿ, plural maḍājiʿ), tagged N. Once the noun-of-place morphology and the surrounding construction are subtracted, the constant left is the notion of the body being laid down / stretched out on its side upon a surface. (1) 32:16 "tatajāfā junūbuhum ʿani l-maḍājiʿ" — "their SIDES (junūb) shrink away from the lying-places": the pairing of junūb (sides) with maḍājiʿ makes the bodily posture explicit — these are the surfaces on which one lays one's side down (beds), and the worshippers pull their sides up off them for night prayer. (2) 4:34 "wa-hjurūhunna fī l-maḍājiʿ" — "forsake them in the lying-places": the marital beds/sleeping-surfaces where the body is laid down. (3) 3:154 "la-baraza lladhīna kutiba ʿalayhimu l-qatlu ilā maḍājiʿihim" — "those for whom killing was decreed would have gone forth to their lying-places": the spots on the ground where their bodies would come to lie (fall slain and stretched out). Across a devotional context (rising off the bed), a marital-legal context (the shared bed), and a battle/decree context (the place of falling dead), the invariant is one and the same: the surface/locus onto which the body is laid recumbent.
DjE.strongest_counterexample: 3:154 (maḍājiʿihim, word_ref 3:154:62:1) is the hardest: here the "lying-places" are not beds of rest but the spots where the slain would fall dead. If the root meant "rest" or "sleep," this would break. It reconciles cleanly under the recumbency reading: the maḍjaʿ is simply where the body comes to lie stretched out — whether in sleep or in death is supplied by context, not by the root. The bodily-lying-down invariant holds without forcing.

E$w.candidate_root_contribution: The dimming/failing of light such that clear seeing lapses — the fading of illumination toward darkness. Concretely realized either in the sky (the darkening end of the daylight span, dusk/nightfall) or in the eye (dimmed, failing sight). The root marks the low-light pole where perceptual clarity is diminished, as opposed to the bright/rising pole.
E$w.plain_explanation: Thirteen of the fourteen occurrences are the temporal nouns ʿishāʾ / ʿashiyy / ʿashiyya, all denoting the dimming, darkening portion of the day — dusk, evening, nightfall. 12:16:3:1 "wa-jāʾū abāhum ʿishāʾan yabkūn" = they came to their father AT NIGHTFALL; 24:58:27:2 "min baʿdi ṣalāti l-ʿishāʾ" = after the ʿishāʾ (night/dark) prayer; 79:46:7:1 "lam yalbathū illā ʿashiyyatan aw ḍuḥāhā" = they tarried only an EVENING or its forenoon. A large sense-family pairs al-ʿashiyy with an explicit morning/rising term, framing it as the DIMMING counterpart to brightening light: 18:28 & 6:52 "bi-l-ghadāti wa-l-ʿashiyy" (dawn/morning ↔ evening), 3:41 & 40:55 "bi-l-ʿashiyyi wa-l-ibkār" (evening ↔ early-morning), 38:18 "bi-l-ʿashiyyi wa-l-ishrāq" (evening ↔ sunrise-shining), 19:11 & 19:62 "bukratan wa-ʿashiyyan" (early-day ↔ evening), 40:46 "ghuduwwan wa-ʿashiyyan" (morning ↔ evening), 30:18 "wa-ʿashiyyan wa-ḥīna tuẓhirūn" (evening, and noon). 38:31:4:3 "ʿuriḍa ʿalayhi bi-l-ʿashiyyi l-ṣāfināt" = the horses were displayed to him in the (declining-light) late-day. Across all of these the root supplies the same thing: the low-light, dimming phase — never the bright/rising phase, which is always carried by a DIFFERENT root standing opposite it. The single verb, 43:36:2:1 "wa-man yaʿshu ʿan dhikri l-raḥmān" = whoever is DIM-SIGHTED toward / turns a blind eye from the remembrance of the Merciful, exposes the more abstract core: yaʿshu is dimmed/failing vision (night-blindness). Subtracting the ʿan-construction (which adds the "away-from" vector) leaves exactly "dimness of sight" — the eye-internal analogue of the sky-external dusk. The concrete image shared by all fourteen is thus failing light and the loss of clear seeing that accompanies it.
E$w.strongest_counterexample: 43:36:2:1 "wa-man yaʿshu ʿan dhikri l-raḥmān" is the hardest, because it is the sole non-temporal, non-nominal occurrence and reads as "turns away from remembrance," which superficially looks like avoidance/aversion rather than "evening." It reconciles cleanly once form and construction are subtracted: yaʿshu is the verb "to have dim/failing vision" (night-blindness); the ʿan adds the directional "away-from." The residue "dimness of sight" is the eye-internal mirror of the sky-external "dimness of light (dusk)" carried by the nouns. The internally-attested bridge is that both are the SAME concrete event — light failing so that clear perception lapses — which is exactly the invariant the nominal cluster already forces. Rather than breaking the unity, 43:36 is what proves the root's core is "dimming of light-for-seeing" and not merely the calendar-slot "evening."

ETw.candidate_root_contribution: The hand-to-hand conveyance of a discrete thing: causing (or effecting) a concrete or reified item to pass into a possessing hand/grasp. The root supplies the "manual transfer of a thing into a hand" — neutral as to direction (into-another's-hand = give, into-one's-own-hand = take/reach); direction is contributed by the derivational form, not by the root.
ETw.plain_explanation: Across all three form-families the invariant is a thing changing hands. The Form IV verb أعطى and the verbal noun عطاء dominate (13/14) and are transparently "hand X over into someone's possession": al-Kawthar conveyed to the Prophet (108:1 أَعْطَيْنَٰكَ ٱلْكَوْثَرَ); Paradise as عَطَآءً غَيْرَ مَجْذُوذٍ, a conveyance "not cut off" (11:108); the Lord's عَطَآء dispensed to both groups and never مَحْظُورًا/withheld (17:20 ×2); every created thing handed its own form (20:50 أَعْطَىٰ كُلَّ شَىْءٍ خَلْقَهُۥ); Solomon's هَٰذَا عَطَآؤُنَا to dispense freely (38:39); the disbeliever who أَعْطَىٰ قَلِيلًا وَأَكْدَىٰٓ — "handed over a little, then held back" (53:34), where the very contrast with withholding shows the root = the act of passing a thing across; the reckoned عَطَآء of the Hereafter (78:36); the pious مَنْ أَعْطَىٰ (92:5); يُعْطِيكَ رَبُّكَ فَتَرْضَىٰٓ (93:5); the charity given/not-given فَإِنْ أُعْطُوا۟ ... وَإِن لَّمْ يُعْطَوْا۟ (9:58 ×2). Crucially 9:29 يُعْطُوا۟ ٱلْجِزْيَةَ عَن يَدٍ makes the "hand" literal ("hand over the jizya out of hand") and shows the root does NOT require benefaction — here the transfer is upward tribute, not a gift. The lone Form VI, 54:29 فَتَعَاطَىٰ فَعَقَرَ ("he took in hand/reached out, then hamstrung"), reverses the vector to take-into-one's-own-hand, confirming that the root itself encodes the hand-conveyance while the form fixes its direction.
ETw.strongest_counterexample: 54:29 (word_ref 54:29:3:2) فَتَعَاطَىٰ فَعَقَرَ — the only occurrence that is not "giving": the villain of Thamud "took in hand / reached out" for the deed (or the sword) and then hamstrung the she-camel. It is the hardest case because its direction is the opposite of the other thirteen (taking, not giving) and its object is diffuse. It reconciles cleanly once the residue is stated as direction-NEUTRAL hand-conveyance: Form VI supplies the "into-one's-own-hand" vector, so the root's own contribution (a thing brought across into a grasp) is still fully recoverable. Indeed this occurrence is the best internal proof that "giving" is form-supplied, not root-supplied.

Ebs.candidate_root_contribution: The contraction/drawing-together of the face into a scowl — a hardening of the countenance into a grim, forbidding, displeased aspect (the "frowning-grimness" residue).
Ebs.plain_explanation: Across all three occurrences the root supplies one invariant: the countenance drawn tight into a grim, forbidding scowl. (1) 74:22:2:1 ثُمَّ عَبَسَ وَبَسَرَ — a human agent "scowled and glared"; عَبَسَ is the facial contraction itself, reinforced by its pairing with بَسَرَ (glaring/grimacing look). (2) 80:1:1:1 عَبَسَ وَتَوَلَّىٰ — again a human "scowled and turned away"; here the root delivers the same facial scowl, while the distinct act of aversion is carried by the separate verb تَوَلَّى (not by ع ب س). (3) 76:10:6:1 يَوْمًا عَبُوسًا قَمْطَرِيرًا — the intensive adjective عَبُوس ("scowling/grim") is predicated of a Day; a Day has no literal face, so the facial-scowl residue is transferred metaphorically to characterize the Day as grim/forbidding in aspect, reinforced by قَمْطَرِير (distressful/harsh). The same grim-forbidding contraction underlies the verbal act (forms 1-2) and the attributive quality (form 3).
Ebs.strongest_counterexample: 76:10:6:1 (يَوْمًا عَبُوسًا) is hardest: a Day cannot literally contract its face. It reconciles by internally-attested metaphorical extension — عَبُوس is the intensive adjectival form of the very scowling act seen verbally in 74:22 and 80:1, and here transfers the "grim/forbidding countenance" to the Day, a transfer reinforced by the paired harshness word قَمْطَرِير. The bridge (facial grimness → grim aspect of an entity) is supported by the shared root-form and does not require external lexicon.

Ehd.candidate_root_contribution: The root contributes the notion of a BINDING COMMITMENT/UNDERTAKING: a solemnly established obligation that binds a party to a stipulated course of action, thereby creating a standing liability to fulfill it (and a corresponding possibility of breach). It denotes neither the future act promised nor the tightness of ratification, but the bond-of-obligation itself — an engagement laid upon or entered into by parties, which stands open to being kept, honored, cast off, or held accountable.
Ehd.plain_explanation:
Across all three form-families the same residue — "a binding obligation/undertaking" — is recoverable once morphology and construction are subtracted.

FORM I (عَهِدَ / أَعْهَدْ, 6 occ.): construed with إِلَى + recipient (+ أَنْ clause), it is a unilateral laying-on of a binding charge. 20:115 "We laid a charge upon (عَهِدْنَا إِلَى) Adam... but he forgot"; 2:125 "We charged (عَهِدْنَا إِلَى) Abraham and Ishmael that: purify My House"; 36:60 "Did I not lay upon you (أَعْهَدْ إِلَيْكُمْ) an engagement that you not worship Satan?"; 3:183 "God bound us by charge (عَهِدَ إِلَيْنَا) that we believe no messenger until..."; 43:49 & 7:134 "by the binding commitment He has with you (بِمَا عَهِدَ عِندَكَ)". In every case the root supplies "a binding obligation established" — the إِلَى frame merely directs it at a recipient.

FORM III (عَاهَدَ, 11 occ.): the derivational reciprocity of Form III supplies mutuality; the root residue is unchanged. 16:91 "when you enter a mutual pact (عَاهَدتُّم)"; 2:100 "whenever they made a covenant (عَاهَدُوا عَهْدًا)"; 33:15 "they had covenanted with God (عَاهَدُوا اللَّهَ) not to turn their backs"; 33:23/48:10 "what they pledged to God upon (عَاهَدُوا اللَّهَ عَلَيْهِ)"; 8:56, 9:1, 9:4, 9:7 "those you made a pact with (عَاهَدتَّ/عَاهَدتُّم)"; 9:75 "covenanted with God that if He gives...". The bond-of-obligation is present throughout; Form III + object (اللَّهَ / مِنْهُم) supplies the counterparties.

NOUN (عَهْد, 29 occ.): names the binding commitment as an object/instrument. The obligation-residue shows in the collocations that presuppose it: fulfilling it — يُوفُونَ بِعَهْدِ اللَّهِ (13:20), أَوْفُوا بِعَهْدِي (2:40), الْمُوفُونَ بِعَهْدِهِمْ (2:177); breaking it — يَنقُضُونَ عَهْدَ اللَّهِ (13:25, 2:27), نَبَذَهُ (2:100); trading it away — تَشْتَرُوا/يَشْتَرُونَ بِعَهْدِ اللَّهِ (16:95, 3:77); being answerable for it — إِنَّ الْعَهْدَ كَانَ مَسْـُٔولًا (17:34), عَهْدُ اللَّهِ مَسْـُٔولًا (33:15); contracting it — اتَّخَذَ عِندَ الرَّحْمَٰنِ/اللَّهِ عَهْدًا (19:78, 19:87, 2:80); its grant — لَا يَنَالُ عَهْدِي الظَّالِمِينَ (2:124); its absence as unreliability — مَا وَجَدْنَا لِأَكْثَرِهِم مِّنْ عَهْدٍ (7:102); paired with entrusted things — لِأَمَٰنَٰتِهِمْ وَعَهْدِهِمْ رَاعُونَ (23:8, 70:32). In each, "binding obligation to be kept" is exactly what can be fulfilled, broken, sold, or asked about.
Ehd.strongest_counterexample: 20:86:16:2 — أَفَطَالَ عَلَيْكُمُ الْعَهْدُ ("did the الْعَهْد seem long/protracted to you?"). Here عَهْد is read by some as an elapsed time-span rather than a pledge, which would threaten the "binding obligation" invariant by substituting a purely temporal sense. It reconciles internally: the immediately preceding clause is أَلَمْ يَعِدْكُمْ رَبُّكُمْ وَعْدًا حَسَنًا ("did your Lord not make you a good promise?"), so الْعَهْد resumes precisely the binding engagement/pledge just named — the sense is "did the [term of the] covenant weigh long upon you," i.e. the obligation and its standing period, not bare chronology. The binding-commitment residue is recoverable, with "duration" supplied contextually by طَالَ, not by the root. A second hard case, بِمَا عَهِدَ عِندَكَ (43:49, 7:134), risks reading as bare "what he knows/has with you," but عِندَ + the pleading "invoke your Lord by..." frames it as the standing commitment God holds with the prophet — obligation-residue intact.

Erw.candidate_root_contribution: A fastening grip-contact: the point or event at which one entity takes firm hold of, or fastens onto, another — either the fixed thing-by-which-a-grip-is-taken (a handhold/loop) or the act of something taking hold of / coming fast upon a person.
Erw.plain_explanation: Two form-families, one invariant. (1) Verb, Form VIII — 11:54:4:1 "ٱعْتَرَىٰكَ بَعْضُ ءَالِهَتِنَا بِسُوٓءٍ": Hud's people say nothing except that "some of our gods have taken hold of / fastened upon you with evil" — an external agent (a deity's harm) grips or comes fast upon the person. (2) Noun ʿurwah — the identical fixed phrase "ٱسْتَمْسَكَ بِٱلْعُرْوَةِ ٱلْوُثْقَىٰ" at 2:256:17:3 and 31:22:10:3: the believer "has grasped the firmest ʿurwah" — the ʿurwah is precisely the handhold/loop, the fixed thing by which a grip is taken and held. Subtract the layers and what both share is not "holding" as an act (that is carried by ٱسْتَمْسَكَ in the noun verses) but the grip-contact / fastening itself: in the verb it is misfortune fastening onto a person; in the noun it is the grip-point onto which one fastens. The root supplies the attachment-contact; morphology and construction supply its direction (something grips me / I grip something) and its polarity (harmful seizure vs. saving hold).
Erw.strongest_counterexample: The verb 11:54:4:1 ٱعْتَرَىٰكَ is the hardest, because its surface sense ("befall/afflict") and its direction of grip are opposite to the nouns: here the person is the one gripped/seized by an external harm, whereas in 2:256 and 31:22 the person is the gripper of a handhold. It reconciles because the direction of the grip and its harmful polarity are supplied by construction (بِسُوٓءٍ) and participants, not by the root; strip those and ٱعْتَرَى still denotes a fastening-taking-hold of one thing upon another — the same grip-contact that ʿurwah names as a fixed point. The residue survives; only its vector is external.

Ery.candidate_root_contribution: The state of being denuded / without a covering — bareness: the absence of a concealing or sheltering layer that would normally overlie a surface (a body, a stretch of ground).
Ery.plain_explanation: Three occurrences, two lexemes. (1) 20:118 تَعْرَىٰ (form I verb, of Adam in the garden): "you will neither go hungry therein nor be uncovered" — the residue is bodily bareness, lacking clothing that covers. (2) 37:145 and (3) 68:49 بِٱلْعَرَآءِ (verbal noun, of Jonah cast ashore): "We cast him onto al-'arā'" — the open, bare tract of ground, land denuded of vegetation and shelter. Across both lexemes the invariant left after subtracting form and context is one thing: a surface stripped of / lacking the covering that would normally overlie it. For the body that covering is clothing (nakedness); for the land it is vegetation/shelter (barren openness). The concept is identical, only the substrate differs.
Ery.strongest_counterexample: The two العَرَآء occurrences (37:145, 68:49) apply the root to LAND, not a body, which could look like a different sense ("open shore/plain") than nakedness. It reconciles cleanly: al-'arā' is precisely the ground "naked" of vegetation and shelter — bareness of terrain — the same denuded-of-covering residue applied to a different surface. No form- or context-forcing is needed; both readings are surface-recoverable as bareness.

HfZ.candidate_root_contribution: The root contributes CUSTODIAL KEEPING: actively maintaining some entity in a preserved, unbreached, un-lost state — holding a charge intact against loss, violation, escape, lapse, or corruption. It is not mere observation and not mere warding-off; it is the vigilant retention/safekeeping of X so that X remains whole and secure under the keeper's responsibility.
HfZ.plain_explanation: Every occurrence, across all five form-families, resolves to "keep X intact / hold X in safe custody." (1) DIVINE PRESERVATION: God is HafiyZ "over all things" (11:57, 34:21, 42:6) — the ultimate custodian; His guarding (HifZ) of the heavens and earth does not tire Him (2:255); He guards the Reminder so it is not lost (15:9); He guarded the heaven from every devil (15:17), a guarding against every rebellious devil (37:7, 41:12), making the sky a "guarded roof" mahfuwZ (21:32). (2) ANGELIC CUSTODY: He sends "keepers" HafaZah over you (6:61); guardians who keep the person yaHfaZuwnahu (13:11); "guardians over you" laHAfiZiyn (82:10); "over every soul is a keeper" HAfiZ (86:4) — custodian-recorders, not idle watchers. (3) HUMAN GUARDIANSHIP: Jacob's sons pledge "we are indeed his keepers" laHAfiZuwn (12:12, 12:63) and "we will keep our brother" naHfaZu (12:65); "God is the best keeper" HAfiZan (12:64); Joseph offers himself as a "keeper, knowing" HafiyZ (12:55) over the storehouses. (4) NEGATED CUSTODY: the Prophet is repeatedly denied the role of custodian/overseer — "we did not send you over them as a keeper" HafiyZan (42:48, 6:107, 4:80), "you have no keeper's charge over them" (83:33), "I am no keeper over you" biHafiyZ (11:86, 6:104) — the residue (custody) is present and simply negated. (5) CHASTITY: those who "keep/guard their private parts" (23:5, 24:30, 24:31, 33:35, 70:29) — holding them inviolate. (6) MAINTAINING PRAYER (form III): "keep up / are assiduous over their prayers" yuHAfiZuwn (23:9, 6:92, 70:34), "keep guard over the prayers" HAfiZuw (2:238) — preserving the observance from lapse. (7) OATHS/LIMITS/COVENANT: "keep your oaths" iHfaZuw (5:89); "keepers of God's limits" al-HAfiZuwn li-Huduwd (9:112); the penitent "keeper" HafiyZ (50:32) — holding a commitment intact. (8) THE ABSENT/UNSEEN: righteous women "guarding the unseen/absent" HAfiZAt lil-ghayb (4:34) "by what God has kept" bimA HafiZa (4:34); "we were not keepers of the unseen" HAfiZiyn (12:81) — safekeeping what is out of sight. (9) PRESERVED RECORD: "a preserving book" kitAb HafiyZ (50:4); "a guarded Tablet" lawH mahfuwZ (85:22) — a record kept intact. (10) ENTRUSTED KEEPING (form X): rabbis/scholars "were made keepers of / entrusted with the Book of God" istuHfiZuw (5:44) — commissioned to hold it in custody. In every case the object is held whole and secure.
HfZ.strongest_counterexample: The form-III "maintain/keep up the prayers" cluster (23:9, 6:92, 70:34, 2:238) is hardest, because here HfZ governs a repeated action, not a possessable object, and reads as "be assiduous/constant." But the residue survives cleanly: to keep up the prayers is to preserve the observance from lapse or loss — the object is held intact over time. The durative/persistent nuance is entirely supplied by Form III's morphology (mufā'ala) plus the 'alā frame, not by the root; strip those and the bare act "keep prayer (from lapsing)" remains custodial keeping. A close second is 4:34:20:1 "bimA HafiZa (A)llāh" ("because of / with what God has kept"), which is elliptical, but its immediate pairing with HAfiZAt lil-ghayb fixes it in the same custody/safekeeping field.

Hrv.candidate_root_contribution: Cultivation-for-yield: the deliberate working of a substrate (ground, and by extension any domain treated as ground) so as to bring forth produce/return — i.e., tillage as a productive enterprise, present either as the act of tilling/sowing (verb) or as the tilled field / its cultivated yield-locus (noun).
Hrv.plain_explanation: Across all 14 occurrences the root names not "crop" as a finished thing, nor "land" as bare ground, but WORKED, YIELD-DIRECTED cultivation. The single verb form makes the act explicit: "Have you seen that which you till/sow (taHruthūna)?" (56:63) — an act of human labor on soil aimed at produce. The literal noun cluster names the tilled field or its cultivated crop as the object/site of that labor: David and Solomon judging over al-Harth into which sheep strayed at night (21:78) — a standing tilled field; the corrupter who "destroys the Harth and the offspring/nasl" (2:205) — cultivation paired with breeding as the two engines of yield; the cow "that does not water/irrigate the Harth" (2:71) — Harth as the irrigated worked field; wind that strikes and destroys "the Harth of a people" (3:117) — the crop-in-cultivation; Harth listed among worldly acquisitions beside cattle (3:14, 6:136, 6:138) — the cultivated holding; "go early to your Harth if you would reap/be harvesters (ṣārimīn)" (68:22) — the field approached precisely for its return. The two metaphorical clusters keep the very same cultivate-for-yield frame and only swap what is cultivated: "Your women are a Harth for you, so come to your Harth as you wish, and send ahead for yourselves" (2:223 ×2) — women figured as the field one tends for offspring, with the forward "send ahead for yourselves" preserving the yield/return vector; and "Whoever desires the Harth of the Hereafter, We increase him in his Harth; whoever desires the Harth of the world, We give him of it" (42:20 ×3) — one's strivings figured as cultivation whose produce is the reward, "We increase him in his Harth" being explicitly the augmenting of a return. Subtracting form (I verb vs. verbal-substantive noun), construction (fī l-Harth locative, iḍāfa harth-hu/harth-kum possessive, harth al-ākhirah genitive-of-domain), participants (David/Solomon, spouses, strivers, wrongdoers), and register (legal, marital, eschatological, polemical) leaves in every case the same residue: substrate worked for produce/return.
Hrv.strongest_counterexample: 2:223 ("Your women are a Harth for you; so come to your Harth as you wish"). It is the hardest because the referent is a person, not soil, so a naive "field/land" gloss fails. It reconciles cleanly under the abstract residue: the woman is figured as the cultivable field the spouse tends, and the yield vector is made explicit in the same breath — "wa-qaddimū li-anfusikum" (send/put forward for yourselves), i.e. cultivate now for a return (offspring). The metaphor operates on the OBJECT of cultivation, not on the root's meaning, which remains "worked substrate directed at produce." A close second is 42:20's "Harth of the Hereafter," equally reconciled by "nazid lahu fī harthihi" — the promise to INCREASE the return names the cultivate-for-yield core outright.

Sdr.candidate_root_contribution: The root contributes the notion of a FRONTMOST / FORE-region that functions as the source-seat of an entity — the leading front-part where its content is held foremost and from which movement or content issues/proceeds forth. In the nominal form it names the chest as this frontal holding-seat of the self; in the verbal forms it names the act of proceeding/being driven forth from a source-point.
Sdr.plain_explanation: Across the 44 noun occurrences صدر/صدور is the chest — but the data consistently exploits it not as mere anatomy but as the FRONTAL SEAT that holds and can release a person's inner content. It is repeatedly the locus of what is contained: 'ما فِى ٱلصُّدُورِ' (100:10; 3:29; 3:154), 'ذَاتِ ٱلصُّدُورِ' — what the chests possess, known only to God (recurring formula: 3:119, 31:23, 35:38, 39:7, 42:24, 57:6, 64:4, 67:13, 5:7, 8:43), 'مَا تُكِنُّ صُدُورُهُمْ' (27:74; 28:69), 'وَمَا تُخْفِى ٱلصُّدُورُ' (40:19; 3:118). It holds ghill/grudge that can be extracted ('نَزَعْنَا مَا فِى صُدُورِهِم مِّنْ غِلٍّ', 15:47; 7:43), rahba/dread (59:13), kibr/arrogance (40:56), need (40:80; 59:9), and is a target of whispering ('يُوَسْوِسُ فِى صُدُورِ ٱلنَّاسِ', 114:5) and healing ('شِفَآءٌ لِّمَا فِى ٱلصُّدُورِ', 10:57; 'يَشْفِ صُدُورَ قَوْمٍ', 9:14). Crucially the chest is presented as the CONTAINER whose fore-position holds the heart: 'ٱلْقُلُوبُ ٱلَّتِى فِى ٱلصُّدُورِ' (22:46) — the qalb sits inside the sadr. As a seat it has capacity that can be constricted or opened: 'يَضِيقُ صَدْرُكَ' (15:97; 26:13), 'ضَآئِقٌ بِهِۦ صَدْرُكَ' (11:12), 'حَصِرَتْ صُدُورُهُمْ' (4:90), 'صَدْرِكَ حَرَجٌ' (7:2), versus opening 'ٱشْرَحْ لِى صَدْرِى' (20:25), 'أَلَمْ نَشْرَحْ لَكَ صَدْرَكَ' (94:1), 'شَرَحَ ٱللَّهُ صَدْرَهُۥ لِلْإِسْلَٰمِ' (39:22; 6:125), 'يَجْعَلْ صَدْرَهُۥ ضَيِّقًا' (6:125). Everywhere the sadr is the frontal seat where the self's states RESIDE at the fore and may be concealed or released. The two verbs make the 'issue-forth-from-source' dimension explicit: 99:6 'يَصْدُرُ ٱلنَّاسُ أَشْتَاتًا' — people proceed/come forth (from the graves/reckoning) in scattered groups; 28:23 (form IV) 'حَتَّىٰ يُصْدِرَ ٱلرِّعَآءُ' — until the shepherds drive their flocks forth (away from the water). The bridge holding all 46 together is the schema FRONT/FORE = SOURCE-POINT-OF-EGRESS: the chest is the leading front-region that serves as origin/seat of what the person holds and lets out; the verb صدر is the pure act of proceeding forth from such a source-point. Both revolve around the same fore-source-and-egress core; only the profiled facet shifts by form.
Sdr.strongest_counterexample: The hardest cases are the pure CONCEALMENT verses — 40:19 'وَمَا تُخْفِى ٱلصُّدُورُ', 27:74/28:69 'مَا تُكِنُّ صُدُورُهُمْ', 3:118 'مَا تُخْفِى صُدُورُهُمْ' — because 'concealing/holding in' looks like the OPPOSITE of 'issuing forth,' which threatens a residue built partly on egress. Reconciliation: the invariant is not 'egress' per se but 'front-region-as-SOURCE-SEAT'; concealment is precisely the seat retaining its content at the fore rather than releasing it. The same seat that can conceal (تُخفي) is the one that can be made to release (نُزع الغل, شفاء لما في الصدور, وسوسة entering it) — holding and issuing are the two poles of one source-seat function, so these verses instantiate rather than contradict the core. The verb 28:23 (drive flocks forth from water) is the mirror case where egress is explicit and 'chest' is absent; it too fits the fore-source-of-egress schema, confirming the abstraction is genuinely shared and not smuggled in from the noun.

Sff.candidate_root_contribution: The root contributes the notion of entities SET INTO A STRAIGHT, ORDERED, SIDE-BY-SIDE LINEAR ARRAY — a rank/row alignment in which parts are held even and extended along a line rather than heaped, scattered, or folded. The invariant is "aligned straight arraying" (linear even-order), independent of who is arrayed or what construction frames it.
Sff.plain_explanation: Across all 14 occurrences the same picture recurs: things brought into an even, extended, linear order. The dominant surface form is the accusative circumstantial noun صَفًّا "(as) a row/rank": humans presented before the Lord صَفًّا (18:48), magicians told to come صَفًّا (20:64), fighters in God's way arrayed صَفًّا "like a welded structure" (61:4), angels standing صَفًّا (78:38) and rank-upon-rank صَفًّا صَفًّا (89:22, two occurrences), and the sworn "arrangers" وَٱلصَّٰٓفَّٰتِ صَفًّا (37:1, both words). The active-participle family names the agents who so array themselves: ٱلصَّآفُّونَ "we are indeed those ranged in ranks" (37:165). The passive-participle family names objects put into rows: سُرُرٍ مَّصْفُوفَةٍ "couches set in rows" (52:20) and نَمَارِقُ مَصْفُوفَةٌ "cushions arranged in rows" (88:15). The camel form صَوَآفَّ (22:36) describes sacrificial beasts drawn up standing in line. Two bird occurrences, ٱلطَّيْرُ صَٰٓفَّٰتٍ (24:41; 67:19), show the same core as extended-straight alignment: 67:19 explicitly contrasts صَٰٓفَّٰتٍ with وَيَقْبِضْنَ ("and they fold/draw in"), so صافّ = wings held out straight and even, the opposite of folding. Whether the aligned units are many bodies in a rank or the two wings of one bird held straight, the residue is identical: held even and extended along a straight line/order.
Sff.strongest_counterexample: The bird occurrences صَٰٓفَّٰتٍ (24:41; 67:19). Here the surface sense could be read as "spreading wings" rather than "multiple entities in a row," which would threaten the row/rank reading. It reconciles cleanly, however, because 67:19 itself supplies the internal bridge: صَٰٓفَّٰتٍ is set against وَيَقْبِضْنَ ("and they fold in"). The contrast shows صافّ = wings held out straight and even (extended in alignment), the antonym of folding/contracting — i.e. the same "held straight and even along a line" residue, applied to the two wings of one body rather than to many bodies. So the harder case actually confirms the abstract core (straight even extension/alignment) rather than merely the concrete "crowd-in-a-line" reading.

SlH.candidate_root_contribution: Being in — or being brought into — a SOUND, FIT, UN-SPOILED right-working condition: intactness / fitness-for-purpose / rightly-ordered wholeness, defined as the positive opposite of fasad (spoilage/corruption). The root itself supplies only this notion of "sound/right condition"; whether it appears as a state (be sound), a quality (that which is sound/fit), or a causation (make sound / set right) is contributed by form, not by the root.
SlH.plain_explanation:
Every form-family recovers the same core "soundness / right-fit condition," differing only by the morphology layered on top.

FORM I (stative) — 13:23 and 40:8 "wa-man salaha min aabaaihim" ("whoever WAS sound/in-right-condition among their forefathers"): the bare verb is the intransitive state of being sound/fit, here fit to enter the Gardens. This is the clearest window on the root: to be in sound order.

PARTICIPLE saalih / saalihaat / saalihuun (the bulk, N/ADJ) — the one/thing IN that sound condition. Applied to deeds: "a deed that is sound/proper/fit" ("aamalan saalihan" 18:110; "al-aamal al-saalih" 35:10; "al-saalihaat" throughout with amiluu).
